13.0.0.en: These verses are recorded in (1 Kgs 15:1, 2, 6) and have been explained, but one difference is noticed here: it is mentioned in the First Book of Kings that Abijah was the son of Maachah the daughter of Absalom, whereas here it says that Abijah was the son of Michaiah the daughter of Uriel. The explanation is that Uriel was not a son of Absalom but the husband of Tamar the daughter of Absalom, so Abijah is the son of Michaiah, the granddaughter of Absalom, who is also called Maachah, as mentioned in (ch. 11:20) and (1 Kgs 15:2). We must know that the Hebrew original of the word "granddaughter" itself means "daughter." The conclusion is that Abijah is the son of Michaiah, who is also called Maachah, and she is the daughter of Uriel, the husband of Tamar the daughter of Absalom; so Abijah is the son of Michaiah, or Maachah, the granddaughter of Absalom.

13.1.0.en: Abijah prepared his army from the kingdom of Judah, and it was four hundred thousand soldiers, while Jeroboam's army was eight hundred thousand soldiers from the tribes, that is, double the army of the kingdom of Judah. But the strength of Abijah and his soldiers lay in their reliance on God and their worship of Him in His holy temple.

13.1.1.en: Reliance on God is able to sustain you in every situation, however difficult. So take care of your repentance and your relationship with God; then you will live in assurance in the face of the devil's wars.

13.1.3.en: 4- And Abijah stood up upon mount Zemaraim, which is in mount Ephraim, and said, Hear me, thou Jeroboam, and all Israel;

13.1.4.en: 5- Ought ye not to know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, even to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt? 6- Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon the son of David, is risen up, and hath rebelled against his lord. 7- And there are gathered unto him vain men, the children of Belial, and have strengthened themselves against Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and tenderhearted, and could not withstand them.

13.1.5.en: 8- And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods. 9- Have ye not cast out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and have made you priests after the manner of the nations of other lands? so that whosoever cometh to consecrate himself with a young bullock and seven rams, the same may be a priest of them that are no gods. 10- But as for us, the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken him; and the priests, which minister unto the LORD, are the sons of Aaron, and the Levites wait upon their business: 11- And they burn unto the LORD every morning and every evening burnt sacrifices and sweet incense: the shewbread also set they in order upon the pure table; and the candlestick of gold with the lamps thereof, to burn every evening: for we keep the charge of the LORD our God; but ye have forsaken him. 12- And, behold, God himself is with us for our captain, and his priests with sounding trumpets to cry alarm against you. O children of Israel, fight ye not against the LORD God of your fathers; for ye shall not prosper.

13.2.0.en: Mount Zemaraim: Zemaraim is a city in the portion of Benjamin and on its border (Josh 18:22). When Abijah found that Jeroboam had attacked him with a great army of eight hundred thousand, he prepared the army of Judah, which was four hundred thousand, as we saw in (v. 3), but he did not rush into the war, because Shemaiah the prophet had warned the kingdom of Judah not to fight the kingdom of Israel, that is, the tribes (ch. 11:4). But he tried to stop the war by going up to Mount Zemaraim, which is on the border of his kingdom, and standing to address Jeroboam and his armies drawn up on the border of the two kingdoms. This shows Abijah's courage and his lack of fear that one of the enemies might shoot him with an arrow.

13.3.0.en: Covenant of salt: salt preserves food, and what is meant by a covenant of salt is a covenant that is not broken or spoiled, that is, a firm covenant.

13.3.1.en: Abijah began to explain to Jeroboam and his armies the reasons that would make the army of Judah triumph over the army of the tribes, and he gave the first proof, which is that God gave an everlasting, firm covenant to David and his offspring, that they might reign over the children of Israel. Here Abijah means that the kingdom belongs to David and his offspring over all Israel, and that the division that occurred was an anomaly, and it would have been right for the tribes to remain subject to the offspring of David, to whom the covenant belongs.

13.4.0.en: Young and tenderhearted: a description of Rehoboam meaning that he was weak like the young and tenderhearted, that is, he did not have the strength and firmness of men, although he was forty-one years old when he began to reign (ch. 12:13). Children of Belial: Belial means Satan, and what is meant is the sons of evil.

13.4.1.en: The second proof of the certainty of Abijah's victory is that Jeroboam was merely a servant of Solomon the son of David, and a rebellious, mutinous servant, who fled to Egypt, then returned in rebellion and gathered wicked men and broke away with the tribes from subjection to the offspring of David, that is, Rehoboam, exploiting his weakness. The meaning of this is that the kingdom belongs to King Abijah, because he is of the offspring of David, and not to the rebellious servant who usurped the kingdom, namely Jeroboam.

13.5.0.en: The third proof is that the kingdom of Judah is the kingdom of the Lord, in the hand of the offspring of David, that is, King Abijah, whereas the kingdom of Israel relied on the pagan gods, namely the golden calves, and relied on the multitude of their number, which is worthless before the power of the Lord; indeed, their worship of the calves will be a cause of the Lord's vengeance upon them.

13.6.0.en: Consecrates himself (fills his hand): offers a sacrifice, that is, devotes himself to the priesthood and becomes a priest. The fourth proof is that the kingdom of Judah relied on the worship of God in His temple and on the official priests, who are of the offspring of Aaron, whereas the kingdom of Israel worshiped idols and relied on priests who were not of the offspring of Aaron as God commanded, but any person who offered a sacrifice became a priest, and they drove out the priests of God, who were of the offspring of Aaron.

13.7.0.en: The fifth proof is the holding fast of the people of the kingdom of Judah to the worship of God in His temple, offering the sacrifices and the offerings, and likewise lighting the lamps and offering incense and sweet spices, that is, offering complete worship to God, and consequently enjoying His care and His unconquerable power.

13.8.0.en: The sixth proof is that God is the true commander of the armies of the kingdom of Judah, and He is the captain before whose power no one can stand, nor before the shout of His priests with the trumpets. Who can fight against God?! And the priests' shout with the trumpets means the presence of God as the commander of His army.

13.8.1.en: In the end he gives advice to the tribes of Israel, led by Jeroboam, which is that they should not attack and fight the kingdom of Judah, because they will be defeated.

13.8.2.en: In the preceding verses Abijah appears in a good light, relying on God and His worship, but in truth he did evil in the sight of the Lord, like Rehoboam his father, and he was not perfect like David (1 Kgs 15:3). But an important question appears: if Abijah walked in evil like Rehoboam, why did God give him victory over Jeroboam? The answer is that God wanted to discipline Jeroboam for his increase in evil, and He used Abijah in that, not because of Abijah's goodness but because Jeroboam's evils were far greater.

13.8.3.en: And although God did not permit Rehoboam to fight the breakaway tribes (ch. 11:4), He permitted Abijah here to fight the tribes and to triumph over them, because of the multitude of the sins of the kingdom of Israel.

13.8.4.en: And we notice a contradiction between Abijah's words and his conduct. In his previous address to Jeroboam, he declares that the Lord is his God and that he has not forsaken Him, although at the same time he allowed the worship of idols, and he rebuked Jeroboam for relying on the golden calves while he himself left the people to worship strange gods, and even allowed idols inside his own house, since his mother Maachah worshiped idols. So Abijah took on the form of godliness while denying its power, and God was angry at this, so his reign lasted only three years.

13.8.5.en: Remember your covenant with God in the sacraments of Baptism and the Holy Myron, and also in the sacraments of confession and Holy Communion, so that you return to God with your heart and walk in what pleases Him, and the devil will not prevail over you.

13.8.7.en: 13- But Jeroboam caused an ambushment to come about behind them: so they were before Judah, and the ambushment was behind them.

13.8.8.en: 14- And when Judah looked back, behold, the battle was before and behind: and they cried unto the LORD, and the priests sounded with the trumpets. 15- Then the men of Judah gave a shout: and as the men of Judah shouted, it came to pass, that God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. 16- And the children of Israel fled before Judah: and God delivered them into their hand. 17- And Abijah and his people slew them with a great slaughter: so there fell down slain of Israel five hundred thousand chosen men. 18- Thus the children of Israel were brought under at that time, and the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the LORD God of their fathers. 19- And Abijah pursued after Jeroboam, and took cities from him, Bethel with the towns thereof, and Jeshanah with the towns thereof, and Ephrain with the towns thereof. 20- Neither did Jeroboam recover strength again in the days of Abijah: and the LORD struck him, and he died.

13.9.0.en: Ambush: a group of soldiers hidden, who appear at the right time to surprise the enemy. Jeroboam did not heed Abijah's warnings, because he relied on two things:

13.9.1.en: 1- The great number of his soldiers, for they were double the number of the soldiers of the kingdom of Judah.

13.9.2.en: 2- His military skill, for he laid a plan for victory, which was setting an ambush.

13.9.3.en: Jeroboam moved with his military plan, and attacked Abijah and did not withdraw despite all of Abijah's warnings to him. At the same time he made a group of his soldiers hide, then circle around, perhaps behind one of the mountains, then circle to come behind the army of Judah, so that the army of Judah would be surrounded in front and behind by the armies of Israel, and they would strike it from the front and from behind, and consequently it would be easy for Jeroboam to triumph over them. So Jeroboam thought.

13.10.0.en: When Abijah found that he was surrounded in front and behind by the armies of Jeroboam, he and all his soldiers cried out to God, on whom they had relied. And the priests sounded the trumpets, to declare that God is the One fighting for Judah, so the soldiers of Judah took courage because of their reliance on God.

13.11.0.en: When the soldiers of Judah grew strong, they shouted, asking for God's help, and when they shouted God answered their prayers, so He intervened and struck Jeroboam and all his army with a blow that made them weak before the soldiers of Judah. The Holy Bible does not mention this blow specifically; it may have been a disease, or a sudden bodily weakness, as He struck the Arameans in the days of Elisha with blindness (2 Kgs 6:18), or fear and terror in the heart, or any other blow, as God had struck the enemies of His people before with stones (Ezek 38:22) or with hornets (Josh 24:12).

13.11.1.en: Prayer is very powerful, especially when it comes from a weak person who seeks God's help with all his heart, for He must intervene. Therefore hasten to God with faith, however great your weakness, that He may fight for you against all adverse circumstances.

13.12.0.en: Abijah was strengthened by the power of God and struck the armies of Jeroboam that were before him and behind him, and killed five hundred thousand of them. Thus Jeroboam was broken, who had tried to subdue and seize the kingdom of Judah relying on his own strength; more than half his army was killed, and he fled in shame before God, the Defender of His children, the people of Judah, who were strengthened when they relied on Him. This is the reward of the believers who relied on their God.

13.13.0.en: Bethel: it lies north of Jerusalem, twelve miles away, and was considered a holy city because God appeared in it to Jacob (Gen 28:19). Jeshanah: a city in the mountain of Ephraim, lying north of the kingdom of Judah.

13.13.1.en: Ephrain: a city lying north of Jerusalem, 8 km away.

13.13.2.en: Abijah continued his victories, so he pursued the armies of Jeroboam and took a number of cities in the south of the kingdom of Israel, that is, near the border of the kingdom of Judah, such as Bethel, Bashan and Ephrain.

13.14.0.en: Jeroboam lived in shame and humiliation after his defeat before Abijah, and could not attack the kingdom of Judah a second time. Then God struck him with a disease that continued for years until he died, two years after the death of Abijah. (4) Abijah's family (vv. 21, 22)

13.14.1.en: 21- But Abijah waxed mighty, and married fourteen wives, and begat twenty and two sons, and sixteen daughters.

13.14.2.en: 22- And the rest of the acts of Abijah, and his ways, and his sayings, are written in the story of the prophet Iddo.

13.15.0.en: When Abijah felt his mighty victory over Jeroboam, he became proud, strengthening himself by his own power, and plunged into his desires, so he married fourteen wives and fathered by them twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. The book does not mention Abijah's sins here, because it is concerned with the plan of salvation, but the Book of Kings tells us that Abijah's heart was not perfect, and despite his good address and his reliance on God, he returned and felt his own strength and relied on himself.

13.15.1.en: Take care to be humble before God and to thank Him at all times for His gifts, so that the devil does not find an opportunity to enter into you, and use the world without plunging into its desires.

13.16.0.en: Midrash: a Hebrew word meaning a book in which interpretations and sermons are recorded.

13.16.1.en: The book tells us here that the details of Abijah's life, his conduct, his words and the meaning they carry were written by Iddo the prophet in a book.

14.0.0.en: Abijah died after reigning over Judah for three years, and they buried him with the kings before him in the city of David, and then his son Asa reigned in his place (1 Kgs 15:9). He was young, but it seems that he had learned reliance on God through the victory of his father Abijah over Jeroboam (ch. 13), and he followed the example of his forefather David (1 Kgs 15:11), whom he regarded as his father, although the surrounding atmosphere was evil, for his father Abijah and his grandfather Rehoboam had walked in evil for no little time, in addition to the fact that his grandmother Maachah worshiped idols and was a strong, dominating personality. Because of Asa's faith and his attachment to God, God gave him security in his kingdom of Judah and put fear in the heart of Jeroboam after his defeat at the hands of Abijah, so Asa lived ten years at the beginning of his reign in security, which helped him in positive works that will appear in the following verses.

14.0.1.en: Do not surrender to evil if it surrounds you in the conduct of those around you, but hold fast to your faith and the commandments of God, even if you are alone with God, for God is able to sustain you, bless your life and bring the wrongdoers into subjection before you.

14.1.0.en: Asa's goodness at the beginning of his reign appears in that he set his aim to please God, so he did what was right and good in His eyes. He did not care to please himself or those around him in order to gain fame or pleasures; therefore Asa is counted among the good kings of the kingdom of Judah.

14.2.0.en: The groves (poles): plural of pole, a piece of wood planted in the ground and rising high, to declare that this place is for the worship of idols, such as Ashtaroth and Baal.

14.2.1.en: Asa's goodness appears in the following:

14.2.2.en: 1- Removing the pagan altars, that is, those of the strange gods.

14.2.3.en: 2- Removing the worship of idols set up on the high places, although the First Book of Kings (1 Kgs 14:15) mentions that the high places were not taken away, because Asa had permitted the offering of sacrifices to God on these high places, as Solomon had done, and this is a mistake, because sacrifices are offered only in the temple of God, and offering sacrifices to God on the high places turns with time into sacrifices being offered to idols on these high places.

14.2.4.en: 3- He broke the images of the pagan idols.

14.2.5.en: 4- He removed the groves that the former kings had set up for the worship of idols.

14.3.0.en: In the days of Abijah, Asa's father, the service in the temple was carried on by the priests and the Levites (ch. 13:

14.3.1.en: 10), but Abijah allowed the worship of idols, and his heart was not perfect before God; therefore after Asa removed the worship of idols, he took care to call the people to worship God and hold fast to His commandments and His law, so that they might remain in life with Him and be rid of the effects of pagan worship and the evils connected with it.

14.4.0.en: Images of the sun: stones or sheets of brass engraved in the form of the sun, set up on pillars, declaring that this place is for the worship of the sun gods. After Asa removed the high places, the worship of the sun gods and the various places of pagan worship, the kingdom of Judah had rest, since the people worshiped God alone in His temple, so God gave them security and rest from all their enemies.

14.5.0.en: Bars: wooden boards set up to secure the gates.

14.5.1.en: Asa seized the opportunity of the kingdom of Judah's rest from the attacks of enemies and took care to fortify the cities with walls, gates and towers. Here Asa's activity and striving appear: he was not lazy because of the rest of the land, but took care to fortify the cities, and God prospered him because of his faithfulness. Asa's reliance was on God, whom he had sought, so He gave the land rest and helped him fortify the cities; that is, he did his part, but his reliance was on God.

14.5.2.en: And building walls to fortify the cities is a type of man's care to guard his senses and thoughts and fortify them with prayer, meditation and spiritual exercises, against the attacks of the enemy, Satan. We notice here that the rest of the land was an opportunity for constructive work, because true rest is in pleasing God and in positive work, and not only in keeping away from sin and the worship of idols. For when a person removes sins by repentance and God gives him rest and helps him, he strives to acquire the virtues, that is, positive work, and he succeeds in all that he does, because God is with him.

14.6.0.en: To complete the positive work, Asa took care to arm the army of the kingdom of Judah, for despite the rest of the land he prepared a great army, numbering three hundred thousand from the tribe of Judah, armed with shields and spears, in addition to two hundred and eighty thousand from the tribe of Benjamin, armed with shields and bows for shooting arrows. From this the importance of constant readiness and spiritual vigilance appears, so that the devil may not find an opportunity or a gap to make us fall into sin.

14.6.2.en: 9- And there came out against them Zerah the Ethiopian with an host of a thousand thousand, and three hundred chariots; and came unto Mareshah.

14.6.3.en: 10- Then Asa went out against him, and they set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah. 11- And Asa cried unto the LORD his God, and said, LORD, it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power: help us, O LORD our God; for we rest on thee, and in thy name we go against this multitude. O LORD, thou art our God; let not man prevail against thee. 12- So the LORD smote the Ethiopians before Asa, and before Judah; and the Ethiopians fled. 13- And Asa and the people that were with him pursued them unto Gerar: and the Ethiopians were overthrown, that they could not recover themselves; for they were destroyed before the LORD, and before his host; and they carried away very much spoil. 14- And they smote all the cities round about Gerar; for the fear of the LORD came upon them: and they spoiled all the cities; for there was exceeding much spoil in them. 15- They smote also the tents of cattle, and carried away sheep and camels in abundance, and returned to Jerusalem.

14.7.0.en: Zerah the Ethiopian (Cushite): a chief or military commander of the Cushites, that is, the Abyssinians, who migrated to the land of the Arabs, that is, Yemen and Saudi Arabia, as proved by Asa's seizing the tents, sheep and camels of the Arabs in (v. 15); or he may have been an Abyssinian commander in Egypt, subject to King Shishak of the Twenty-Second Dynasty, who gathered a great army of Egyptians and with them mercenaries of the Cushites and Libyans, famous for their strength in war (16:8). Mareshah: a city lying in a plain southwest of Jerusalem.

14.7.1.en: Valley of Zephathah: a valley next to the city of Mareshah.

14.7.2.en: Zerah the Cushite attacked with a great army, numbering a million soldiers and armed with many weapons, among them three hundred war chariots, to seize the kingdom of Judah, and he encamped near Mareshah. So Asa went out with an army from the kingdom of Judah and met the army of Zerah in the valley of Zephathah.

14.8.0.en: Because Asa was a good king, he prayed to God, declaring his faith in Him, that He is able to work with the few as with the many, that is, able to give the small army of Judah victory over the great army of Zerah, and he declared his reliance on God, that is, Asa did not move to meet Zerah except relying on the power of God.

14.8.1.en: And so Asa's success appeared in this test of faith, because he relied on God and did not fear the power and the multitude of Zerah's army.

14.8.2.en: The importance of Asa's preparation in the days of peace, which lasted ten years, also appeared here. Satan does not surrender, and although God restrained him for ten years, he renews the attack. And because Asa had become accustomed to prayer in the days of peace, it was easy for him to seek God in the distress of Zerah's attack on him, and God answered him, as He had answered in the days of peace, and he triumphed over Zerah.

14.8.3.en: And we find Asa's humility clear, for he described himself as having no strength before the multitude of Zerah's army, so his only reliance was on God, although the number of Asa's army was not small, for it was five hundred and eighty thousand warriors, strongly armed, yet he relied on God and not on his army.

14.8.4.en: And we also find Asa's faith clear, in his feeling that God is his own God, who cannot possibly abandon him, so it mentions that he "called on the Lord his God."

14.8.5.en: Humility is the shortest way to the tender heart of God, so declare your weakness before Him and ask for His help, and you will be able to overcome all the powers of evil.

14.9.0.en: Gerar: a city south of Jerusalem, 100 km away.

14.9.1.en: After the prayer Asa advanced and engaged the army of Zerah, and triumphed over it and killed most of the army, so that the Holy Bible mentions here that no living person was left of it, that is, most of Zerah's soldiers were killed. And Asa pursued the army of Zerah a long distance, about 100 km, to Gerar, killing many of the enemies there and taking their spoil, which was a reward from God to Asa for his faith and for his striving. So we see in Asa the necessity of combining spiritual striving with prayer, that is, striving with grace, so that we may obtain victory and the divine reward.

14.9.2.en: And God's quickness in answering His children in distress appears clearly, for He rescues them and rewards them.

14.10.0.en: The army of Zerah tried to take refuge in some of the cities around Gerar, so Asa struck them in order to destroy the army of Zerah. He also struck the tents of the Arabs in the valleys, in which the Cushites tried to take shelter. And he took much spoil from the Arabs and these cities, whether camels, sheep or tents, in addition to all kinds of spoil, and they returned victorious to Jerusalem. Perhaps some of Zerah's army had its home in these tents of the Arabs, and in this way Asa destroyed and wiped them out in their own homeland. Asa's revival (1) Azariah's warnings (vv. 1-7)-

14.10.1.en: 1- And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: 2- And he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.

14.10.2.en: 3- Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law. 4- But when they in their trouble did turn unto the LORD God of Israel, and sought him, he was found of them. 5- And in those times there was no peace to him that went out, nor to him that came in, but great vexations were upon all the inhabitants of the countries. 6- And nation was destroyed of nation, and city of city: for God did vex them with all adversity. 7- Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded.
